summary.text: The proof expresses the numerator’s prime valuation as \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor^2\) and the denominator’s as \(\sum_{i\ge1}G(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor)\), where \(G(M)=\sum_{r=1}^M r\lfloor M/r\rfloor\); the bound \(G(M)\le M^2\) also shows the quotient is exact. For \(m=np+k\) with \(0\le k<p\), every \(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\) for \(i\ge1\) equals \(\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\), so both product valuations—and hence their difference, the quotient valuation—are unchanged.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 N(m)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\prod_{r=1}^{m}\gcd(j,r),
 \qquad
 D(m)=\prod_{r=1}^{m}\left(\left\lfloor\frac m r\right\rfloor !\right)^r.
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is
\[
 a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)},
\]
where initially the fraction is interpreted as integer division. We will first prove that the division is exact, and at the same time obtain formulas for the prime-adic orders of its numerator and denominator.

For a prime \(q\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in a positive integer \(x\). We use the standard facts
\[
 v_q(xy)=v_q(x)+v_q(y),\qquad
 v_q(\gcd(x,y))=\min(v_q(x),v_q(y)),
\]
and Legendre's formula
\[
 v_q(t!)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
All sums indexed by \(i\geq1\) below are in fact finite, since their terms vanish once \(q^i\) exceeds the relevant integer.

Define the auxiliary arithmetic function
\[
 G(M)=\sum_{r=1}^{M}r\left\lfloor\frac Mr\right\rfloor.
\]
We will prove the two formulas
\[
 v_q(N(m))=\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2, \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
 v_q(D(m))=\sum_{i\geq1}G\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor\right). \tag{2}
\]

We begin with (1). By additivity of valuations over products and the valuation formula for a greatest common divisor,
\[
 v_q(N(m))
 =\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m}\min(v_q(j),v_q(r)).
\]
For any two positive integers \(j,r\),
\[
 \min(v_q(j),v_q(r))
 =\sum_{i\geq1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}\,{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid r}. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, the summand is one precisely for those positive \(i\) satisfying both \(i\leq v_q(j)\) and \(i\leq v_q(r)\), and hence there are exactly \(\min(v_q(j),v_q(r))\) such indices. Substituting (3), interchanging the finite sums, and separating the sums in \(j\) and \(r\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_q(N(m))
 &=\sum_{i\geq1}
   \left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}\right)
   \left(\sum_{r=1}^{m}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid r}\right)\\
 &=\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last equality uses the elementary fact that the number of multiples of a positive integer \(d\) among \(1,\dots,m\) is \(\lfloor m/d\rfloor\). This proves (1).

For (2), apply additivity of valuations, the rule \(v_q(x^r)=r v_q(x)\), and Legendre's formula:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_q(D(m))
 &=\sum_{r=1}^{m}r\,v_q\left(\left\lfloor\frac mr\right\rfloor!\right)\\
 &=\sum_{r=1}^{m}r\sum_{i\geq1}
       \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/r\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
For positive divisors, iterated integer division satisfies
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/r\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m}{r q^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor}{r}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently, after interchanging the finite sums,
\[
 v_q(D(m))
 =\sum_{i\geq1}\sum_{r=1}^{m}
 r\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor}{r}\right\rfloor.

a
For fixed \(i\), put \(M=\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\). If \(r>M\), then \(\lfloor M/r\rfloor=0\); therefore the inner sum may be truncated at \(M\), and it is exactly
\[
 \sum_{r=1}^{M}r\left\lfloor\frac Mr\right\rfloor=G(M).
\]
This proves (2).

For completeness, these formulas can be viewed entirely as finite formulas. Choose any integer \(B\) larger than the largest possible \(q\)-adic valuation of an integer at most \(m\), for example any \(B>\log_q m\) when \(m>0\). Then every sum over \(i\geq1\) above can be written as a sum over \(1\leq i<B\). Indeed, if \(q^i\mid x\leq m\), then \(q^i\leq m\), so \(i\leq\log_q m\). Thus all rearrangements used above are rearrangements of finite sums. The case \(m=0\) is harmless as all defining products are empty and the relevant sums vanish.

We next prove that \(D(m)\) always divides \(N(m)\). The key estimate is
\[
 G(M)\leq M^2. \tag{4}
\]
For every \(1\leq r\leq M\),
\[
 r\left\lfloor\frac Mr\right\rfloor\leq M,
\]
because \(r\lfloor M/r\rfloor\) is the largest multiple of \(r\) not exceeding \(M\). There are \(M\) terms in the definition of \(G(M)\), so summing this inequality gives (4). It also holds for \(M=0\), when the sum is empty.

Applying (4) term by term to (2), and comparing with (1), gives, for every prime \(q\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_q(D(m))
 &=\sum_{i\geq1}G\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor\right)\\
 &\leq\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2
 =v_q(N(m)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Both \(N(m)\) and \(D(m)\) are positive: every greatest common divisor occurring in \(N(m)\) is positive, and every factorial occurring in \(D(m)\) is positive. The prime-factorization criterion for divisibility now implies
\[
 D(m)\mid N(m). \tag{5}
\]
Thus the quotient defining \(a(m)\) is an exact positive-integer quotient. From (5) and multiplicativity of valuations,
\[
 v_q(N(m))=v_q(a(m))+v_q(D(m)), \tag{6}
\]
for every prime \(q\). Equivalently, one may write \(v_q(a(m))=v_q(N(m))-v_q(D(m))\), since the second valuation is no larger than the first.

We now prove the desired block constancy. Let \(n\) be a positive integer, let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy
\[
 0\leq k<p.
\]
The elementary observation driving the proof is that for every \(i\geq1\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor. \tag{7}
\]
To see this, first divide by \(p\). Since \(0\leq k<p\), Euclidean division gives
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
For \(i\geq1\), division by \(p^i=p\,p^{i-1}\) can be performed by first dividing by \(p\) and then by \(p^{i-1}\). Dividing the two equal quantities in the preceding display by \(p^{i-1}\) proves (7).

Apply numerator formula (1) with \(q=p\), first to \(m=np\) and then to \(m=np+k\). By (7), corresponding summands agree for every \(i\geq1\):
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\]
Hence
\[
 v_p(N(np+k))=v_p(N(np)). \tag{8}
\]
Likewise, apply denominator formula (2). Again (7) shows that the argument of \(G\) is the same in every corresponding summand, so
\[
 v_p(D(np+k))=v_p(D(np)). \tag{9}
\]

Finally use (6) at \(m=np\) and at \(m=np+k\):
\[
 v_p(N(np))=v_p(a(np))+v_p(D(np)),
\]
\[
 v_p(N(np+k))=v_p(a(np+k))+v_p(D(np+k)).
\]
The left sides are equal by (8), and the denominator valuations are equal by (9). Cancelling these equal terms yields
\[
 v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+k)).
\]
This holds for every \(k=0,1,\dots,p-1\). Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
 =\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))
 =\cdots
 =\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
as claimed.
